DevOps Principles: Culture, collaboration & shared ownership; the development-operations divide

slides.title: Shared Ownership Defined
slides.lead:
DevOps is a working culture where the team that writes code also helps run it in production, instead of handing it off and walking away
The formal term, DevOps (Development + Operations), names this merged way of working

points.text: Collaboration: developers and operations plan releases together
Shared ownership: dev and ops jointly own production reliability

slides.notes: "Open by asking why a team that only writes code might ship fragile software. Stress that DevOps is a culture and set of practices, not a single tool or job title. Interviewers often ask to define DevOps in one line — this slide is that line."

slides.title: Shared Ownership Defined

points.text: Feedback loop: production issues flow straight back to coders
Automation mindset: manual handoffs replaced by shared pipelines

slides.notes: "Open by asking why a team that only writes code might ship fragile software. Stress that DevOps is a culture and set of practices, not a single tool or job title. Interviewers often ask to define DevOps in one line — this slide is that line."

slides.label: Analogy: a group project with one shared grade
slides.title: Shared Ownership Defined
slides.notes: TR analogy: In a group project where everyone gets the same grade, no one says 'my part was fine': just as in DevOps, Dev and Ops share the result, so both work together to make the software run well. "Open by asking why a team that only writes code might ship fragile software. Stress that DevOps is a culture and set of practices, not a single tool or job title. Interviewers often ask to define DevOps in one line — this slide is that line."

slides.title: Why Teams Split
slides.lead:
Before this culture spread, developers were measured on shipping new features fast, while operations staff were measured on keeping systems stable
This gap, known as the development-operations divide, pulled the two goals in opposite directions

points.text: Conflicting incentives: speed for developers, stability for operations
Wall of confusion: code thrown over with no runtime context

slides.notes: "Explain the 'wall of confusion' as the historical root cause DevOps was invented to remove. Mention that this silo problem is the classic interview question: why did DevOps emerge. Keep this grounded in the incentive mismatch, not tooling."

slides.title: Why Teams Split

points.text: Blame game: outages blamed on 'bad code' or 'bad infra'
Slow releases: manual handoffs and approvals delayed every deployment

slides.notes: "Explain the 'wall of confusion' as the historical root cause DevOps was invented to remove. Mention that this silo problem is the classic interview question: why did DevOps emerge. Keep this grounded in the incentive mismatch, not tooling."

slides.title: Practices And Location
slides.lead: Shared ownership turns into concrete practice through the principle that teams building a service share responsibility for operating and supporting it in production

points.text: Blameless postmortems: incidents reviewed for process, not people
On-call rotation: developers share production support duty
Shared dashboards: both teams watch the same metrics
AWS CodePipeline and CodeDeploy consoles: shared release visibility

slides.notes: "Point out that naming CodePipeline here is the real-world anchor, even without a live demo. Emphasise blameless postmortems as a frequently asked culture question in interviews. Keep this distinct from tooling mechanics, which come later."

slides.title: Bridging Forward
slides.lead: Shared ownership only works once the steps from writing code to running it are defined as one continuous flow, not separate handoffs

points.text: Culture sets the goal: one team, one responsibility
The software delivery lifecycle turns that goal into stages
Each stage removes one more manual handoff point

slides.notes: "Close by framing culture as the 'why' before the lifecycle shows the 'how'. Ask the class to recall which incentive mismatch caused the divide, as a quick recall check. Keep this bridging line short and declarative."
The Cloud SDLC: Plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate & monitor

slides.title: Eight-Stage Pipeline
slides.lead: Shipping software only works if every change moves through the same sequence of checks, from an idea to a running feature; cloud tools and automation help teams move each change through this sequence consistently
slides.notes: "Point to the looping arrow from Monitor back to Plan to show this is a continuous cycle, not a one-time process. A common interview question asks to name the SDLC stages in order."

slides.title: Eight-Stage Pipeline

cells: Requirements and user stories defined before coding
Source written and committed to a repository
Source and dependencies compiled into an artifact
Automated checks verify the artifact before it proceeds
Tested artifact is versioned and marked ready
Release artifact is pushed to a target environment
Running system is managed in production
Metrics and logs watched for problems, feeding back into planning

slides.notes: "Point to the looping arrow from Monitor back to Plan to show this is a continuous cycle, not a one-time process. A common interview question asks to name the SDLC stages in order."

slides.title: Defining Work First
slides.lead: Before any code exists, the plan stage turns a business need into clear requirements and user stories, so developers know what to build

points.text: Plan output: backlog items, acceptance criteria, sprint goals
Code stage: developers write source and commit to a shared repository

slides.notes: "Explain the backlog as a prioritised to-do list the plan stage produces, and note that a commit hands work from Plan into Code. Interviewers may ask why planning counts as its own SDLC stage."

slides.title: Defining Work First

points.text: Issue trackers like Jira link each commit to its requirement
Typical location: source lives in a hosted Git repository, such as GitHub

slides.notes: "Explain the backlog as a prioritised to-do list the plan stage produces, and note that a commit hands work from Plan into Code. Interviewers may ask why planning counts as its own SDLC stage."

slides.label: Analogy: an architect's blueprint before the bricks
slides.title: Defining Work First
slides.notes: TR analogy: A construction project needs an architect's blueprint before workers lay a single brick: just as the plan stage fixes requirements before the code stage starts building. "Explain the backlog as a prioritised to-do list the plan stage produces, and note that a commit hands work from Plan into Code. Interviewers may ask why planning counts as its own SDLC stage."

slides.title: Automated Verification
slides.lead: Once code is committed, the build stage turns it into a single deployable artifact, and the test stage runs automated checks on that artifact before anything moves further

points.text: Build: compiles source, resolves dependencies, produces one packaged artifact
Tests cover unit level logic and integration between components

slides.notes: "Point to the pass/fail fork and stress that an artifact never reaches release without passing its tests. A frequent interview question asks what the build stage actually produces — one versioned artifact, not just compiled files."

slides.title: Automated Verification

points.text: A failing test stops the artifact from moving to release
AWS location: CodeBuild runs the compile and automated-test steps

slides.notes: "Point to the pass/fail fork and stress that an artifact never reaches release without passing its tests. A frequent interview question asks what the build stage actually produces — one versioned artifact, not just compiled files."

slides.title: Shipping The Artifact
slides.lead: A tested artifact still needs two separate steps to reach users: release marks it ready and versions it, deploy actually moves it onto a running environment

points.text: Release: tested artifact is tagged, versioned and stored in a registry such as Amazon ECR
Deploy: the released artifact is installed on servers or containers

slides.notes: "Clarify that release and deploy are distinct actions, not synonyms — a release can sit ready without being deployed yet. Flag that the dev, staging, production sequence shown here returns when delivery and promotion are taught."

slides.title: Shipping The Artifact

points.text: Target environments: development, staging and production, in that order
AWS location: CodeDeploy automates deployment to EC2, ECS or Lambda

slides.notes: "Clarify that release and deploy are distinct actions, not synonyms — a release can sit ready without being deployed yet. Flag that the dev, staging, production sequence shown here returns when delivery and promotion are taught."

slides.title: Running In Production
slides.lead: Once deployed, the operate stage keeps the live system healthy through scaling and incident response, while the monitor stage watches it continuously for trouble

points.text: Operate covers patching, capacity changes and on-call incident response
Monitor: metrics, logs and alerts track health in real time

slides.notes: "Point to the feedback arrow and explain that monitoring data becomes input for the next planning cycle, not a dead end. Interviewers often ask how monitoring differs from operating — operate keeps the system running, monitor tells the team when it is not."

slides.title: Running In Production

points.text: AWS location: CloudWatch collects metrics and triggers alerts
Monitoring signals feed back into planning, closing the SDLC loop

slides.notes: "Point to the feedback arrow and explain that monitoring data becomes input for the next planning cycle, not a dead end. Interviewers often ask how monitoring differs from operating — operate keeps the system running, monitor tells the team when it is not."
Version Control & Git Workflows: Repositories, branches, commits & merges; pull requests & code review; trunk-based vs feature-branch

slides.title: Tracking Code Changes
slides.lead:
Multiple developers editing the same codebase without a system overwrite each other's work and lose history
Git, the distributed version-control system nearly all teams use, solves this by recording every change as a traceable snapshot

points.text: Repository: the project folder plus its complete change history
Branches: separate lines of work inside the same repository

slides.notes: "Open with the overwritten-work problem before naming Git. Point out that GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket all host repositories built on this same model. Interview angle: ask what a repository actually stores besides the current files."

slides.title: Tracking Code Changes

points.text: Commits: saved snapshots forming the project's timeline
Pull requests: reviewed proposals to merge one branch into another

slides.notes: "Open with the overwritten-work problem before naming Git. Point out that GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket all host repositories built on this same model. Interview angle: ask what a repository actually stores besides the current files."

slides.title: Snapshots And Lines
slides.lead:
A commit is a snapshot of the exact file state at one point, identified by a unique hash
A branch is a named, movable pointer to a sequence of commits, letting one line of work diverge from another

points.text: HEAD: pointer marking the commit currently being worked on
main: the default branch holding the stable, deployable codebase
Branching cost: near-instant, since a branch is only a pointer

slides.notes: "Stress that a branch is only a pointer, not a copy of all files, which is why creating one is instant. Ask: what moves when HEAD switches branches? Mention the GitHub branch-switcher dropdown as where this is seen live."

slides.label: Analogy: photographs and a second album
slides.title: Snapshots And Lines
slides.notes: TR analogy: A commit is like a photograph of the project at one moment, and a branch is a separate photo album started to try a new idea without touching the main album: just as a Git branch lets commits diverge safely before rejoining the original history. "Stress that a branch is only a pointer, not a copy of all files, which is why creating one is instant. Ask: what moves when HEAD switches branches? Mention the GitHub branch-switcher dropdown as where this is seen live."

slides.title: Combining Branch Histories
slides.lead:
Once a branch's changes are ready, merging brings them back into another branch, usually main
Git either fast-forwards the pointer when histories have not diverged, or creates a merge commit joining two separate histories

points.text: Fast-forward merge: target branch had no new commits of its own
Merge conflict: same lines changed differently, needs manual resolution
Merge commit: a new commit that joins two diverged branch histories

slides.notes: "Explain a conflict as Git refusing to guess which change is correct, leaving markers in the file for a human decision. Ask: why does rebase rewrite commit history while merge does not? Mention that a pull request merge button runs this same merge, or a squash or rebase variant of it."

slides.title: Proposing Merges Safely
slides.lead:
A pull request (PR) asks reviewers to approve a branch's changes before they merge into main, turning a merge into a checkpoint instead of a silent action
Code review is that check: teammates read the changes to catch bugs and share context before the merge

points.text: Diff view: shows exactly which lines changed, line by line
Review comments: reviewers flag issues before approving the merge

slides.notes: "Point to the diff view and the green approve button as the two things reviewers actually act on. Explain code review as a second pair of eyes catching bugs and sharing context before code reaches main. Interview hook: why block merges on required approvals rather than trusting the author?"

slides.title: Proposing Merges Safely

points.text: Required approvals: a rule blocking merge until reviewers sign off
Status checks: automated results displayed directly on the request

slides.notes: "Point to the diff view and the green approve button as the two things reviewers actually act on. Explain code review as a second pair of eyes catching bugs and sharing context before code reaches main. Interview hook: why block merges on required approvals rather than trusting the author?"

slides.title: Trunk vs Feature Branch
slides.lead: Teams choose a branching workflow to structure how changes move into main; the two dominant patterns trade merge frequency against isolation

cells: Frequent releases, automated build and test on every merge

slides.notes: "Trunk-based is the pattern most continuous-integration setups assume, so flag that connection without defining CI yet. Ask: why does a long-lived feature branch make merge conflicts worse over time? Keep this AWS-agnostic since it is a Git workflow choice, not a provider feature."

slides.title: Trunk vs Feature Branch

points.text: Trunk-based needs feature flags to hide incomplete work safely
Feature-branch isolates risk but delays integration problems
Short-lived feature branches blend both approaches in practice

slides.notes: "Trunk-based is the pattern most continuous-integration setups assume, so flag that connection without defining CI yet. Ask: why does a long-lived feature branch make merge conflicts worse over time? Keep this AWS-agnostic since it is a Git workflow choice, not a provider feature."

Mid-session quiz (sections 1-3). Q1. Define DevOps in one line. Answer: A working culture where the team that writes code also helps run it in production. Q2. What was the wall of confusion? Answer: Code thrown over to operations with no runtime context. Q3. Name the eight SDLC stages in order. Answer: Plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, monitor. Q4. What does the build stage produce? Answer: One packaged, versioned artifact. Q5. Why is creating a Git branch near-instant? Answer: A branch is only a pointer to a commit. Q6. When does Git fast-forward instead of creating a merge commit? Answer: When the target branch had no new commits of its own. Q7. Which branching workflow keeps conflicts small? Answer: Trunk-based, with branches living hours to a day.
Continuous Integration: Build & test on every change; fast feedback; cost of a broken main branch

slides.title: Merge Without Breaking
slides.lead:
A merge pushed without a check can silently break code many developers depend on
Continuous Integration (CI) builds and tests every change the moment it is pushed, catching problems early

points.text: Triggered automatically by every push or pull request
Runs an automated build to compile or package code

slides.notes: "Explain CI as an automatic check on every push, not an end-of-day review. Point to GitHub Actions as where this pipeline is configured. Exam hook: CI means build and test triggered on every commit."

slides.title: Merge Without Breaking

points.text: Executes the full test suite against the new change
Common CI tools: GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI, AWS CodeBuild

slides.notes: "Explain CI as an automatic check on every push, not an end-of-day review. Point to GitHub Actions as where this pipeline is configured. Exam hook: CI means build and test triggered on every commit."

slides.label: Analogy: a restaurant checks each dish
slides.title: Merge Without Breaking
slides.notes: TR analogy: A restaurant checks each dish before serving it to customers, rather than waiting until the end of the day to discover problems: just as CI builds and tests every code change immediately to catch issues early. "Explain CI as an automatic check on every push, not an end-of-day review. Point to GitHub Actions as where this pipeline is configured. Exam hook: CI means build and test triggered on every commit."

slides.title: On Every Change
slides.lead: Each commit triggers the loop on its own, so a developer learns within minutes whether a change broke something, while the code is still fresh

points.text: Checkout: CI server pulls the exact commit pushed
Build: code compiled or dependencies installed fresh
Unit tests run first, since they are fast and isolated

slides.notes: "Stress that fast feedback means catching a bug in minutes rather than weeks later during release testing. Point out the pass/fail badge shown on a pull request. Exam hook: fast feedback shortens the gap between introducing and detecting a bug."

slides.title: On Every Change

points.text: Result posted directly on the pull request as pass or fail
Fast feedback: CI results reach the developer in minutes, not hours, so bugs are fixed while the change is fresh

slides.notes: "Stress that fast feedback means catching a bug in minutes rather than weeks later during release testing. Point out the pass/fail badge shown on a pull request. Exam hook: fast feedback shortens the gap between introducing and detecting a bug."

slides.title: Why It Matters
slides.lead: A failing main branch blocks every teammate who branches from or merges into it, turning one bad change into a team-wide stoppage

points.text: Every teammate pulling main inherits the broken code
Deployments pause until the breakage is resolved
Teams fix-forward or revert to limit the blast radius

slides.notes: "Emphasise that a broken main branch is costly because it stops the whole team, not just one developer. Point to the red cross on a GitHub Actions check as the visible signal. Exam hook: why branch protection ties merge ability to a passing CI run."

slides.title: Why It Matters

points.text: Branch protection rules require CI to pass before merge
Visible on GitHub Actions as a failing status check

note.text: A passing build only confirms the code compiles and passes its automated tests; moving that verified artifact onward into delivery is the next concern

slides.notes: "Emphasise that a broken main branch is costly because it stops the whole team, not just one developer. Point to the red cross on a GitHub Actions check as the visible signal. Exam hook: why branch protection ties merge ability to a passing CI run."
Delivery & Artifacts: Continuous delivery vs continuous deployment; build once & promote; dev, staging & production

slides.title: From Build To Release
slides.lead: Continuous Integration confirms every change builds and passes tests; what happens after that merge decides when and how the change actually reaches users

points.text: Continuous delivery: code always release-ready, release needs manual trigger
Continuous deployment: every passing change auto-releases to production

slides.notes: "Frame this as the stage right after CI's build-and-test gate passes. Point out the four terms on screen as the section map. Flag the interview trap: both continuous delivery and continuous deployment abbreviate to CD."

slides.title: From Build To Release

points.text: Build once: one artifact built once, never rebuilt per environment
Promotion: the same artifact moves through dev, staging and production

slides.notes: "Frame this as the stage right after CI's build-and-test gate passes. Point out the four terms on screen as the section map. Flag the interview trap: both continuous delivery and continuous deployment abbreviate to CD."

slides.title: Automatic Vs Manual
slides.lead: Continuous delivery, CD, packages every tested change for release but keeps a human approval gate; continuous deployment, also called CD, removes that gate and releases automatically the moment tests pass

points.text: Delivery: release decision stays manual, triggered on demand
Deployment: release triggered automatically, no human in the loop

slides.notes: "Stress that the automated steps before this point are identical; only the final gate differs. Ask: why would a team choose to keep the manual gate even with full test coverage? Mention compliance or customer-facing risk as the usual answer."

slides.title: Automatic Vs Manual

points.text: Both require the same passing automated test suite first
Deployment suits mature pipelines with strong automated test coverage

slides.notes: "Stress that the automated steps before this point are identical; only the final gate differs. Ask: why would a team choose to keep the manual gate even with full test coverage? Mention compliance or customer-facing risk as the usual answer."

slides.title: Automatic Vs Manual

points.text: Release frequency: delivery releases on demand; deployment releases several times a day
Pipeline set-up: delivery adds a manual approval stage; deployment has none

slides.notes: "Stress that the automated steps before this point are identical; only the final gate differs. Ask: why would a team choose to keep the manual gate even with full test coverage? Mention compliance or customer-facing risk as the usual answer."

slides.label: Analogy: a software update, approved or automatic
slides.title: Automatic Vs Manual
slides.notes: TR analogy: A software update is prepared and tested before reaching users. In continuous delivery, it waits for a person's approval before going live; in continuous deployment, it goes live automatically after passing all tests: just as the difference is whether a human approves the release or the pipeline handles it automatically. "Stress that the automated steps before this point are identical; only the final gate differs. Ask: why would a team choose to keep the manual gate even with full test coverage? Mention compliance or customer-facing risk as the usual answer."

slides.title: Same Artifact Everywhere
slides.lead:
Rebuilding code separately for each environment risks a staging-only quirk slipping into production
Build once and promote avoids this by compiling a single artifact carried unchanged through every stage

points.text: Artifact built once, tagged with a unique version such as app:a1b2c3d that is never reused
Same binary or container image tested in staging, then promoted

slides.notes: "Point to the artifact box staying identical across every stage, nothing rebuilt in between. Say plainly: rebuilding per environment can silently produce a different binary than what was tested. Exam hook: ask why build-once-promote matters for reproducible releases."

slides.title: Same Artifact Everywhere

points.text: Promotion copies the artifact forward with no recompilation
Stored in a repository, for example Amazon S3 or ECR

slides.notes: "Point to the artifact box staying identical across every stage, nothing rebuilt in between. Say plainly: rebuilding per environment can silently produce a different binary than what was tested. Exam hook: ask why build-once-promote matters for reproducible releases."

slides.title: Same Artifact Everywhere

points.text: Environment differences, such as URLs and credentials, come from external configuration, not a rebuild
Guarantees the code tested is exactly the code released

slides.notes: "Point to the artifact box staying identical across every stage, nothing rebuilt in between. Say plainly: rebuilding per environment can silently produce a different binary than what was tested. Exam hook: ask why build-once-promote matters for reproducible releases."

slides.title: Environment Pipeline Roles
slides.lead: Each environment plays a distinct role in catching problems before customers do, so an artifact earns its way to production only by passing through every stage in order

points.text: Dev: integration testing, frequent deploys, lowest stability requirement
Staging: mirrors production configuration, final verification before release

slides.notes: "Name the CodePipeline console as where these stages are literally configured, one after another. Point to the gate between staging and production as the same approval step from the earlier slide. Exam hook: ask why staging must mirror production configuration closely."

slides.title: Environment Pipeline Roles

points.text: Production: serves real users, promotion gated by approval or tests
AWS CodePipeline models each environment as a separate pipeline stage

slides.notes: "Name the CodePipeline console as where these stages are literally configured, one after another. Point to the gate between staging and production as the same approval step from the earlier slide. Exam hook: ask why staging must mirror production configuration closely."

Quiz on DevOps & CI/CD Fundamentals. Q1. Why did DevOps emerge? Answer: Developers were measured on speed and operations on stability, so the two goals pulled apart. Q2. What is a blameless postmortem? Answer: An incident review of the process, not the people. Q3. Is a release the same as a deploy? Answer: No, a release can sit ready without being deployed yet. Q4. What do reviewers act on in a pull request? Answer: The diff view and the approve button. Q5. What triggers a CI run? Answer: Every push or pull request. Q6. Why is a broken main branch costly? Answer: It stops the whole team, not just one developer. Q7. What is the one difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment? Answer: Delivery keeps a manual approval gate before production; deployment has none. Q8. Why build once and promote? Answer: The code tested is exactly the code released.
